Overview

Younger Bloomington residents faced low awareness of planning meetings and proposals that were hard to picture. My HCI/d capstone explored a mobile way to understand neighborhood projects and contribute ideas.

Resident and planner research led to a simulated neighborhood, ready-made design elements, and proposal feedback. The current prototype adds a categorized builder and progress updates; six residents tested the original 2025 concept.

Key Impact

6 residents tested the concept

Participants saw potential for inclusive community engagement and identified two usability refinements. This is qualitative feedback on the 2025 prototype; participation growth and the current revision’s usability remain unmeasured.

The problemWhat research changedExploring directionsTesting & iterationExperience the solutionWhat changedReflection

A proposal cannot invite input if people cannot picture it.

Bloomington’s existing input channels included newsletters, surveys, council meetings, and design presentations. Research exposed gaps in awareness, convenience, and visual context. I narrowed a broad urban-design ambition to community projects and civic-oriented residents aged 18–35.

How might we help younger residents understand neighborhood changes and contribute ideas that planners can interpret?

Connect a resident’s perspective to a planner’s decision.

4 planning interviews6 resident interviewsSecondary research + digital ethnography

I combined resident and planning perspectives to define what useful participation needed. The findings connected barriers in the current process to specific interface decisions.

From documented findings to design implications
EvidenceDesign implication
Low awareness and inconvenient participation.Let residents explore projects beyond a meeting.
Proposals shown without enough spatial context.Locate a proposed change in its neighborhood.
Feedback could be misinterpreted.Pair comments with visual ideas and project context.
Research scope and constraints

Digital ethnography covered Reddit, public forums, and government websites. A workshop involved 4 participants plus me; paper-concept comparison involved 2 city planners and 2 users. Participant overlap across activities is unknown. Digital confidence, input overload, and trust in representation remain constraints.

Keep the context of a place. Add the freedom to propose.

A workshop with four participants explored three directions. After comparing paper concepts with two city planners and two users, I developed the simulation approach: contextual feedback plus a way to build an idea.

Explored · Kiosk

Build together, in person.

Collaborative blocks at City Hall offered shared discussion, tied to organized sessions.

Explored · AR

Overlay a proposal on a place.

An AR concept connected feedback to a resident’s view of the physical site.

Selected · Simulation

Explore, respond, and create.

A virtual neighborhood combined proposal feedback with resident-built ideas in one experience.

Inspect the original wireframes

Testing made choice and feedback the next priorities.

Six Bloomington residents tested the 2025 high-fidelity prototype. Their feedback identified two refinements. The later mobile app makes these ideas tangible, with further testing still needed.

Choosing an element
2025 findingPrefab elements needed clearer organization.
Later changeBuildings, Outdoors, and Mobility categories give the library structure.
Recognizing a result
2025 findingA new design’s arrival in the plot needed emphasis.
Later changePlacement feedback and a submission preview show the result of an action.

These are different prototype versions and screen formats. The current revision has no documented retest; the changes remain hypotheses to evaluate.

Explore, propose, and follow what happens next.

The current app translates the concept into three connected mobile flows. Snapping sheets balance the map with project details; a bounded element library makes a proposal approachable.

01 · Understand a project

Explore → Hopewell West → expand the sheet. Read context before contributing.

02 · Put an idea in place

Design this space → choose or drag an element → Review idea. A limited library reduces the blank-page task.

03 · Stay involved

Notifications → My proposals. A reference, next step, and review stage explain what follows.

Try the mobile prototype

Load the working app to explore these flows. Activity stays in this browser; street views, committee messages, and review progress are simulated. Proposals are not sent to the council.

Six residents saw potential. Participation impact remains unmeasured.

6Bloomington residents tested the 2025 prototype

Positive qualitative feedback.

Participants saw value in a more inclusive way to engage and surfaced two actionable usability refinements.

The evidence supports a promising concept. It does not establish city adoption, participation growth, or validated improvements in the current app.

A digital channel needs a representative conversation.

Architecture taught me that a proposal changes everyday life. This project taught me to narrow the question enough to test it—and to consider whose input reaches a decision.

Ready-made elements lower the barrier to proposing, while limiting what residents can express. Next, I would test the revised builder and feedback flow across different levels of digital confidence, then work with planners on interpreting conflicting input. Outreach and a credible review process need to grow alongside the interface.
